learn.title: Disaster recovery design: RPO, RTO and Azure Site Recovery
objectives: Derive RPO and RTO from business statements and tier workloads so each gets a recovery design it can afford
Choose a DR strategy (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active) by trading cost against RPO and RTO
Design Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure, VMware/physical and Hyper-V to Azure, including replication policy, recovery plans, test failover and failback
Plan network and DNS failover, target capacity, and the choice between paired and non-paired regions
Recommend DR for PaaS services with their own geo-replication and govern the whole estate with Azure Business Continuity Center
concepts: Recovery point objective (RPO)
The maximum amount of data, measured in time, that the business can afford to lose. 'We can lose at most 15 minutes of orders' means an RPO of 15 minutes.
Recovery time objective (RTO)
The maximum time a workload can be unavailable after a disaster before it must be running again. It includes detection, decision, failover, start-up and DNS or client redirection.
Availability vs recoverability

Availability keeps a workload running through small failures (zones, instances). Recoverability brings it back after a large event (region loss, corruption, ransomware). A zone-redundant design still needs a DR plan.
Azure Site Recovery
An Azure service that replicates Azure VMs between regions or zones, and VMware VMs, physical servers and Hyper-V VMs to Azure, and orchestrates failover and failback.
Crash-consistent recovery point
Disk data as if the power were pulled. Site Recovery creates one every 5 minutes and you cannot change this. Good enough for file, print and DHCP servers.
App-consistent recovery point
Also captures in-memory data and in-flight transactions, using VSS on Windows or custom scripts on Linux. Minimum frequency is 1 hour. Recommended for databases such as SQL Server.
Replication policy
Defines recovery-point retention and app-consistent snapshot frequency. The default is 1 day of retention and no app-consistent snapshots. The oldest usable point is 15 days with managed disks.
Recovery plan

Groups machines (up to 100 protected instances) into ordered groups. Machines in a group fail over in parallel, groups run in order, and you can add scripts, Azure Automation runbooks and manual actions.
Test failover
A DR drill that creates VMs from a recovery point in a network you choose, ideally isolated, while replication continues and production is untouched. Clean up the test afterwards.
Failback and reprotect

After failover, reprotect replicates the recovered VMs back toward the original site, then a failover in the reverse direction returns the workload. Physical servers can only fail back to a VMware VM.
Region pair

Two regions in the same geography (Brazil South is the exception) with sequential platform updates and prioritised recovery in a broad outage. Site Recovery can replicate between any two regions, paired or not.
Azure Business Continuity Center
A unified management experience for Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery that shows protection status, finds unprotected resources and helps govern BCDR at scale.
comparisons: Backup and restore vs pilot light

Backup and restore is cheapest but has an RPO up to the backup interval and an RTO of hours, because everything is rebuilt. Pilot light (for example Site Recovery) keeps data replicated with no running compute, so RPO is minutes and RTO is much shorter.

Warm standby runs a scaled-down copy in the second region that is scaled up at failover. Active-active runs full capacity in both regions behind a global load balancer for near-zero RTO, at roughly double the cost.

Site Recovery protects whole VMs with crash-consistent points every 5 minutes and app-consistent points at best hourly. SQL Server Always On or Azure SQL geo-replication gives transaction-level RPO of seconds for the database tier.

Paired regions give sequential updates, prioritised recovery and are the fixed target of GRS. Non-paired regions are fine for Site Recovery and app-level replication, but GRS cannot target them, so use options such as object replication.
A test failover runs in a chosen network, does not shut down the source and does not stop replication. A real failover moves production to the target and is followed by commit and reprotect.
Site Recovery is for ongoing disaster recovery with failback. Azure Migrate is for one-way migration to Azure.
traps: Zone redundancy, availability sets and scale sets are high availability, not disaster recovery: none of them survive the loss of a whole region.
Site Recovery failover is not automatic. Someone (or your own automation) must start it, so detection and decision time count toward RTO.
Replication copies corruption and ransomware encryption almost immediately. Recovery from logical damage needs older recovery points or backups.
An app-consistent RPO tighter than 1 hour cannot be met with Site Recovery alone; use database-native replication.
Run test failovers into an isolated virtual network, not the production one, to avoid IP, DNS and Active Directory conflicts.
Site Recovery does not protect PaaS services such as App Service or Azure SQL Database; those use their own multi-region or geo-replication features.
revision: RPO = how much data you can lose; RTO = how long you can be down.
Cost rises from backup and restore, to pilot light, to warm standby, to active-active.
Site Recovery: crash-consistent every 5 minutes, app-consistent every 1 hour at best, default retention 1 day, maximum 15 days.
Every protected instance is free of Site Recovery charges for its first 31 days; storage and compute are still charged.
Recovery plans order the start-up of tiers and automate post-failover steps to shrink RTO; test each app's plan regularly.
Hyper-V VMs replicate as often as every 30 seconds; Azure VMs, VMware VMs and physical servers replicate continuously.
Use capacity reservation in the target region when failover capacity must be guaranteed.
Lower DNS TTLs and use Traffic Manager or Front Door so clients follow the workload to the DR region.
